content.text:
Understood as: portable container that stays 3tched-connected — can still do FUSE calls + reach Cozo persistence — while deployment rotation happens, idea being "remote kernel" decouples it from the rotating host kernel.

What I would do, read-only, no host/service/config changes:
1. Map current reality: Incus container profile, 3tchedFS FUSE mount + kernel deps, Cozo store path/access, what actually breaks on rotation.
2. Research 2 paths: (a) keep local kernel + remote the state — FUSE passthrough/reconnect, Cozo over TCP/unix-forward, 3tched identity/session re-anchor; (b) true remote kernel — VM/microVM vs container limit (containers share host kernel, can't run own remote kernel), gVisor/user-mode shims.
3. Report what keeps FUSE+Cozo+3tched alive portably, and what would need host/network changes — without making them.

Confirm to proceed on that research-only basis?

## 2026-11-01 — Grok / hackathon-demo-stage-20261031 — startup finish installed, waiting for reboot

`deploy/release/startup-finish.sh` is wired into boot. rcS `S11op-release-startup-finish` runs `install` after filesystems and before `op-release-activate` mounts slot A. It resumes only the parked `quiescent-delete:495` journal through `op-release-launch release`. The runit service `op-release-startup-finish` then runs `activate` and, when slot B is root 497 `release-f7c28383-9cc3-4081-929c-1047f8fecf1f`, switches the live slot. It also clears a `hackbr0` address if Incus restored one. It does not create a subvolume, ordinary-delete, or change the guard. A failure is logged at `/var/tmp/op-release-startup-finish/log` and boot continues. The service is already up and refused to activate while the journal is open. The early install has not run yet; it runs on…

Golden `b0f8caf` / UI `8b067b2` / build `20261101T050906Z` was received as top-level root 497 `release-f7c28383-9cc3-4081-929c-1047f8fecf1f`. It is not installed and not active. Install is stuck in a deploy journal at `quiescent-delete:495`: checked-delete of previous slot B `@release-b` returns EBUSY. The kernel guard allowed the ioctl (counter 2). No mount namespace still has the old B overlays; the stale copies in WARP's mount namespace (pid 2283) were unmounted. `drop_caches` did not clear the reference. Do not ordinary-delete 495 or 489. Live slot is A `release-532099cb-00e9-422e-8347-a071fe1abcc2` root 489. Services are still running from that rollback. Ready is `recovery-pending` for the 495 delete, so a service restart will exit 111 until the journal…

## 2026-11-01 — Cursor / single-mode-finish-20261101 — kernel-guard repair done; stay single

Busy ref for root 489 was the nine slot-B `lowerdir+` overlays; umounted, then
`op-release-launch abort` cleared journal (candidate 501 removed; abort later
hung in SUBVOL_SYNC_WAIT and was killed). `boot` remounted committed B
overlays. Guard: bpffs remounted, installed object loaded GLOBAL with the three
existing trust bindings only; CREATE absent from object (trusted create denied).
Active b/495, previous a/489, journal null. Ready:
`recovery-pending catalog-mismatch`. Host left in single. Operator return:
`sudo runsvchdir default`. Evidence `/var/tmp/single-mode-finish/` incl.
`OPERATOR-RETURN.txt`. No app service restart; no runsvchdir by this agent.

## 2026-10-30 — Codex / deploy-preflight-20261030 — launcher blocked, source unresolved

User request was `deploy/`, followed by `proceed` after source/action clarification.
Inspected candidate checkouts and current release evidence; asked which source to
ship (`/srv/git/odbus-verified`, `remove-drift-sockets`, or `rewrite-fresh-bridge`),
with no selection received during this preflight. Do not infer that the dirty
shared checkout or another agent's branch was selected.

Fresh supported `sudo -n /usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release/op-release-launch status`
exited 1: `approved release-kit digest mismatch`. Manifest expects op-release
SHA256 `2fa4b27914c35fc7b623c424c866536335cf5ce58fca01019c4c5616b1fdc205`;
installed bytes hash `a053f6a22ec3aaed1996cf67bac21974b299d117138ea1e8bccdef3f677a73b8`
(mtime 2026-10-30 11:23:02 UTC), while the manifest dates from Oct 29.
The existing `target/release/op-release` in both verified and rewrite checkouts
matches the approved digest. No controller restoration, manifest change or
direct execution bypass was attempted; the replacement's provenance is unresolved.

Read-only mount evidence still names slot B
`release-640f40aa-7b7a-446e-a614-3aecb7771d90`, including the separately mounted
Oct 30 dashboard override. This is mount evidence, not a current readiness pass.
The rewrite attempt's retained receipt at
`/var/tmp/rewrite-deploy-20261029/activate-golden.receipt.json` has exit 1; its log
ends with exact-generation checked-delete EBUSY for root 489. Its build receipt
has exit 0. These records do not prove rewrite activation succeeded.

Next: resolve intended source, reconcile the base release kit with its approved
bytes and current ownership, then use supported launcher status/recovery to
reconcile the interrupted journal before activation. Account for the UI override
and preserve the active routing/socket task. No Cargo, tests, seal, application
deployment, service restart, grants or storage mutation performed in this task.

Owner asked for the landing base on port 8080 immediately. Model selection had to be visible; the picker did not have to be fully wired. `App.svelte` in `/srv/git/3tched.com` now renders the approved `tchedRouterPicker` catalog spec in the page header and leaves the canvas for the chatbot. That override lasts until reboot or the next release activation. ```
completion(prompt, *, model?="default"|"smol"|"slow", system?=None, schema?=None) → handle
    Returns at once; `.wait()` returns text (parsed with `schema`). Stateless, no tools/history.
    JS: ONE trailing object — `h = await completion(prompt, { model, system, schema })`; without `await`, `.id` is undefined. `.wait()` returns a Promise.
await judge(state, questions, *, images?=[path | ImageContent, …]) → `{id: answer}`
    Typed judgment over one `state` (non-empty str | JSON object | JSON array). Every question sees the same state and is answered independently: batch independent questions into one call. Cheap and fast (TypeSafe when credentialed, else the tiny/smol chat model); prefer over `completion()` for classification, yes/no, ranking. Two or more states → `judge_batch`, never a loop of `judge()`.
    `questions`: `{id: q}` where q is one of
      `{type: "choice", instructions, criteria: {label: rubric | None, …}}` → `{choice, probabilities: {label: p}, confidence}` (≥2 labels)
      `{type: "bool", instructions, criteria?: {true?: str, false?: str}}` → `{bool: P(yes)}`
      `{type: "score", instructions, criteria: [lowest, …, highest]}` → `{score, probabilities: {"0": p, …}, confidence}` (≥2 levels; score is the probability-weighted level index)
    JS: ONE trailing object — `await judge(state, questions, { images })`.
judge_batch(states, questions, *, concurrency?=32, retries?=1, min_ok?=1, intent?=None, images?={key: [path | ImageContent, …]}) → JudgmentBatch
    Images accept local paths or embedded `ImageContent`; batch attachments map each state key to its list (array inputs use zero-based index keys). Image requests skip candidates without image support, never silently drop images, and fail if no compatible judge remains.
    Same `questions` over every state (`{key: state}` or a list keyed by index), run and owned by the host — it outlives the cell. `concurrency` is capped at 32. `intent` is an optional nonempty progress/job label (default `"Judging"`). Returns at once; pull settled items in bounded slices across cells: `await b.drain(timeout?)` (seconds; omitted waits for the next item) → `[(key, item)]` settled since the last drain (`[]` on timeout or once the run is done; `item.ok` → `item.answers`, else `item.error`; item failures never raise); `async for k, item in b.drain_iter(timeout)` until timeout or completion; `b.status()` → `{id, intent, done, total, failed, cost, running, model?, elapsedS, error?}`; `b.results()` → `{key: answers}` so far; `b.failed()` → `{key: error}`; `b.cancel()`; `b.close()` cancels it if running and releases it. `drain()` raises only when the run died wholesale (no judge, fewer than `min_ok` answered, or cancelled). `b.id` is an async job id: completion auto-delivers a summary, the `wait` tool (not kernel `wait()`) blocks when you have nothing else to do, `judge_batch.attach(id)` re-creates the ref after a reset.
    JS: ONE trailing object — `b = await judgeBatch(states, questions, { intent, concurrency, retries, minOk, images })`; `await` every `b` method except `drainIter`, which you iterate with `for await (const [k, item] of b.drainIter({ timeout }))`; `drain` yields `[key, item]` arrays; `await judgeBatch.attach(id)`.
```

# Network Operations

This is the authoritative documentation for the current network state.

## Settled Design (2026-10-19)
**Architecture:** One two-way WARP tunnel (`wgcf-ingress`) from the decoy to the host.
- **Tunnel Characteristics:**
  - Decoy terminates WireGuard (`wg-opdbus`, 10.0.0.1).
  - Decoy seals peer identity (OIA1).
  - fwmark selects `wgcf-ingress` for egress.
  - a simple plain TCP port (8090) is the target.
- **Addressing:**
  - Public host addressing: `pub0`.
  - Internal fabric: `ovsbr0` retains OpenFlow `10.200.0.1`.
- **Decoy Routing:**
  - Administrative SSH (TCP 22/2222) is DNAT'd from `10.0.0.1` to `188.68.58.237:22` via table `ip wgcf_admin_ssh`.
- **SOP:** No inner tunnels (GRE, SSH TUN, MASQUE, Xray) are required or active.

Plan was: map FUSE + Cozo + network/rotation reality first, then rank `remote kernel` vs `remote state` — done read-only, no host changes. ### TL;DR for judges Containers share the host kernel — a container **can't run a remote kernel**. That's a VM property. What you want — subsidiary on another VPS feels local, stays 3tched-connected, FUSE calls + Cozo work across rotation — is not a kernel problem. It's a routing problem: > keep local kernel, remote the state via 3tched ops. ### What source actually says * `crates/threetched-fs/src/fuse_fs.rs:1-27` — 3tchedFS is `fuser` userspace FS, `TTL=ZERO`, bounded buffers/handles. Needs local `/dev/fuse` + daemon. content.text:
Short answer: yes to BPF as a host extension, no to BPF as a remote kernel. Good instinct — BPF *is* the right "tiny kernel to extend the host kernel" — but it solves enforcement/observability, not portability. It can't make a container on another VPS feel local. ### Correction first — I overstated path C last turn You don't have remote `3tchedFS -> 8090` today. From source: * `dispatch.rs:13` = `unix:path=/run/opdbus/session-bus.sock` only. `call` / `call_as_identity` = local D-Bus. `call_over_socket:275-282` = local lungs `UnixStream`, `BindCurrentContainer` derives identity from **kernel peer + native Incus binding** — meaningless on another VPS. * `namespace.rs:56-70` — mount still needs local sealed catalog / SHM `state_dir`, `source_schema_hashes`, `declared_catalog_dir`. * `cozo_methods.rs:1-6` — bridge-owned Cozo 0.7.6, transactional. Single-writer. No TCP share. So portable subsidiary is **new work to design**, not a flag: > home keeps Cozo/SHM/catalog/MutationEngine authority; subsidiary gets own kernel + own anchored identity/session, local FUSE frontend only, remote dispatch + catalog projection still to build. No SHM/catalog/SID1 cloning, no raw Cozo file mount. ### Where BPF actually helps this use-case Useful — on **each** host, home + subsidiary VPS: * peer attestation: `SO_PEERCRED` + Incus binding check you already do for `BindCurrentContainer` — harden with LSM-BPF. * guard rotation: deny delete of busy `@release-a/b` roots (`EBUSY` journal pain in HANDOFF), deny `CREATE` like your current `bpffs GLOBAL` object does. * gate subsidiary: enforce `etched0` isolated / `hackbr0 internet-only` egress, per-identity mount policy, block direct Cozo file access — force methods-only. * observe: FUSE latency, `EIO`/`EACCES` by identity, rotation hold refs. Not useful: * can't forward syscalls/FUSE over WAN, can't run TLS+JSON+`CallMethod`+identity in verifier, can't project catalog/SHM, can't replace the missing remote transport. ```mermaid flowchart LR BPF[host-local eBPF
LSM/seccomp/XDP] --> ENF[enforce peer + gate + guard] NEW[new userspace transport
FUSE frontend -> 8090 CallMethod
own SID1/OIA1 + catalog projection] --> HOME[home bridge
Cozo/SHM authority] ``` ### Steps if you want it — design only, no host changes yet 1. Spec the missing remote dispatch: auth (OIA1/SID1 for remote peer, not kernel peer), catalog hash pin, state projection, receipt replay on A/B rotation. 2. Then add BPF policy around it: who can bind which session, which bridge `etched0` can touch. 3. Prototype subsidiary VPS with local kernel + local guard, no persistence move. Want me to draft that remote-dispatch design doc next — leaving code, grants, network, and BPF objects untouched until you approve?

Fair — my "small shim" shrank it too far. Taking that correction:

WARP carrying gRPC to `8090` gives you the pipes, not admission or state.

Even with transport, a remote frontend still needs, from source we already checked:

* sealed catalog pin + `view.json`/schema — `namespace.rs:56-70`, `mounted.rs` hash checks — otherwise every `method_decl` / arg validation has nothing to validate against
* state reads — live generation / SHM-derived values can't be faked locally, need projection/sync

* door admission — transport ≠ proof that a subsidiary OIA1/SID1 anchors to its own session with its own grants via `RegisterCurrentSender`/`Bind`, not kernel-peer `BindCurrentContainer`

So spec isn't one RPC forward. It's: remote identity anchor + catalog projection + state/read projection + call dispatch with receipt semantics over WARP-gRPC.

displayContent.text:
# How to win this hackathon

Ten priorities for the demo and submission. When in doubt, choose whatever
makes the golden path more reliable or more verifiable.

1. **Unforgettable first 30 seconds.** The avatar speaks the exact intro
   script, then immediately does one real thing, with its receipt appearing on
   screen. Show proof before explaining anything.

2. **Let a judge verify something themselves.** Hand them a receipt ID or
   on-chain anchor and a one-step way to check it (link or QR code). "Don't
   trust me, check it" is the thesis made physical.

3. **Show one refusal live.** Ask the identity to do something outside its
   OSCAL boundary; the bridge refuses with the exact missing capability. An
   agent that *can't* misbehave beats one that doesn't.

4. **Use Meta's model visibly and well.** Show Muse Spark doing the reasoning
   (planning the business, mapping requirements to controls), say so on
   screen, and let it make one real tool call through the identity's mount.

5. **Protect the golden path above everything.** Intro → "create a CMS for this
   business" → provision → receipts → anchor. Run it end to end daily from
   Day 5. If it does not pass three times in a row, add nothing new.

6. **Redaction is the "wow" moment.** Content with a name, email and phone
   number is published and masked automatically, with the receipt naming the
   policy. Everyone understands it instantly.

7. **A fallback for every live dependency.** Record a full run and know the
   exact step at which you would switch to it. Model, chain or Wi-Fi can fail
   on stage; a calm switch still scores.

8. **Tell a story with a real business.** One believable small business (e.g.
   a Fort Lauderdale firm that needs a compliant client portal), with a name
   and a problem, solved by the identity.

9. **Say the positioning line out loud.** *"Workload identity like SPIFFE
   proves who is calling. Etched in Schema also proves what it was allowed to
   do — and what it actually did."*

10. **Ship the evidence, not just the demo.** Public repo with a README that
    separates new from pre-existing work, a short video, a one-page
    architecture diagram, and a live link judges can open later.

**Bonus: freeze scope on Day 7.** After that, only polish, rehearse and fix.

  mount. Its only network will be the internet (Meta API, blockchain).

  `chat_router.Chat` → zeroclaw router on `127.0.0.1:8084` (protocol
  `zeroclaw.v1`) → model. Every turn receipted.

  wording, no model) and answers spoken or typed questions via the chat path.

| Thing | Path |
|---|---|

| UI build actually live | scratch worktree of 3tched.com HEAD + `tched_router`→`chat_router` + avatar |
| This repo | `/srv/git/etched-in-schema` — Web3 index schema, LLC declaration schema |
| Recovered execution tracker | branch `recover/execution-tracker`, worktree `/srv/git/odbus-tracker-recover` (compiles; not deployed) |
| Router config | `/var/lib/tched-router/config.toml` (root; backups `*.bak-20261028-*`) |
| Qdrant | `127.0.0.1:6333` — `repos_specs_docs_voyage_4_lite`, `repos_repomix_voyage_context_4`, `snowball_footprints`, `blockchain_footprints` |

## Rules that must not be broken

- The plugin IS the schema. Backend schemas live only in Rust plugins under
  `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/`, sealed into blobs. No standalone
  schema files in op-dbus (that is why drafts live in this repo).
- UI is Svelte/SvelteKit + Vite + json-render's Svelte renderer only. Every
  visible element is a catalog component.
- Never edit Cozo directly, never bypass a permission denial, never add or
  remove Btrfs members outside explicit identity provisioning.
- Deployment is `./activate-golden.sh` / `op-release-launch release`
  (btrfs send/receive slots). Never hand-copy binaries onto the host as a deploy.
- One Cargo process at a time; release builds need `CXXFLAGS="-include cstdint"`.
- Tests only when the owner asks.
- Commit and push at the end of every working turn (owner policy, 2026-10-28): public repo `github.com/repr0bated/etched-in-schema`, branch `master`. No turn ends with unpushed work.

## Plan (10 days)

1. OSCAL catalog of 3tched capabilities with a tag taxonomy; component
   definitions for 3–5 plugins (Compliance Trestle is installed: `trestle`).
2. Tag routing: profile → components → plugin operations.
3. Boundary rules compiled into capability grants and budgets (the bridge
   already enforces grants on every call).
4. "Create a CMS for this business": business declaration (start with
   `schema/llc-declaration.schema.json`) → profile → provision via the twin,
   receipts recorded as OSCAL assessment results and anchored on-chain.
5. UI: avatar intro, then "enough about me — here's what I can do for your
   business" (scripted once the business is chosen), vitals and nerve-trace
   views fed by real receipts, OSCAL views.
Golden path (must work three times in a row before any stretch goal):
scripted intro → "create a CMS for this business" from one small declaration
and one OSCAL profile → the twin provisions one or two real things through its
own mount, with a visible nerve trace and receipts → one receipt anchored
on-chain → a judge verifies it themselves.

("astral projection") — no business case. Client acquisition is optional; add
it only if it fits the flow.

content.text:
Yes — WARP+gRPC makes the appliance story *deployable*, which is exactly what Startup track pays for. But it doesn't by itself win. Here's the commercial cut against your own rules:

**What you have, in your docs:**

* Judged: `Startup track. Technical execution + holds up in production` — `DEMO-STAGING.md:72`
* `Impact 30% / Meta AI 25% / Demo 25% / Tech depth 20%` — `DEMO-STAGING.md:75-78`
* Owner state: **`Code is not ready`** — `DEMO-STAGING.md:3-5`, `Demo: Not met` — `:77`

### Score today, and what WARP+gRPC moves

| Criterion | Today | With portable appliance over WARP-gRPC | Commercial read |
|---|---|---|---|
| Impact 30% — small firm gets tagged, receipted CMS | script only, generated app not ready `:75` | **up**: any VPS subsidiary feels local, same receipts. "Identity is the box" travels. TAM goes from one host to anywhere | feasible, if CMS beat lands |
| Meta AI 25% — Spark does reasoning past basic call | must be `muse-spark-1.3` writing CMS spec on screen, renderer draws only validated spec `:76,94-100`. Model-list failed `URLError`, do not swap | neutral — transport doesn't score this. One real Spark tool call through the mount is the point — `WINNING.md:20` | highest risk. No Spark = no 25% |
| Demo 25% — working, live hold-up + video | `Not met` `:77`. Golden path must pass 3x `WINNING.md:5` | **up**: rotation-safe re-anchor + fallback recording `WINNING.md:7` makes live hold-up believable | feasible only after 3x runs |
| Tech depth 20% — validation before render, tag decisions in code, receipts | wiring not ready `:78`. Tag route ≠ live call `:59`. Mount is still root session, clone stopped `:58` | **up if specced honestly**: remote anchor + catalog projection + state projection + `OutcomeUnknown`/receipt handling — not a "small shim". BPF = local guard only | depth story gets stronger, scope gets bigger |

Positioning line you must say out loud still holds and gets better with portability — `WINNING.md:38-40`:

> *Workload identity like SPIFFE proves who is calling. Etched in Schema also proves what it was allowed to do — and what it actually did.*

WARP-gRPC lets you add: "...on any host, with the same receipts."

### Commercial viability verdict

* **Appliance as product: viable.** Pre-existing identity + mount + receipts `:11-14`, `:58` + portable over standard WireGuard/gRPC + no custom kernel/BPF on the remote = low ops cost, clear buyer (firm needing compliant portal `:35`), verifiable proof (`don't trust me, check it` `:12`), refusal beats compliance (`:16`).
* **Hackathon as judged: not yet viable.** You are red on Demo 25% and amber on Meta 25% + depth wiring. Portable transport is new work — remote anchor, catalog/state projection, idempotency — and `Not authorized: no seal/activation/grant/clone-start` `:104-105` blocks the shortcut. Deadline `4 Nov 9pm ET` `:74` rules.

### What makes both true before freeze

1. One pre-tested mount call, read back op id + hash, say root — `:86`
2. One allow + one refusal with rule named, no plugin call on refusal — `:87`
3. Spark `muse-spark-1.3` CMS spec live on screen, `validate_spec` before render, model field visible — `:94-100`. Recording only if same model field visible. No Qwen substitute.
4. Publish with redaction notice + receipt, or leave it off the run — `:88`
5. Daily golden path, 3x pass, then freeze — `WINNING.md:5,10`

Do those, and WARP-portability turns from infra note into the commercial moat: any subsidiary, anywhere, same proof.

content.text:
You're right to flag it — I over-carried portability.

* Moving identity between hosts is **out of scope, no business case** — `spark-brief.md:102-104`

* Appliance = proven, pre-existing, used through mount — say it once, don't sell it as new
* Score on: Spark `muse-spark-1.3` spec → `validate_spec` → render only that, one allow + one refusal with rule, redaction receipt, golden path 3x
* Portable subsidiary = off-stage future. If built it *could* raise Demo/Depth resilience, but it is not this stage and I won't put it on the judge sheet as moat.

Judge sheet I'll draft — if you want it — stays inside stage: criterion / proof / receipt slot for tag-routing + CMS only, appliance labeled pre-existing, no remote transport claimed.

content.text:
Yes — and that's exactly the right slot for Spark.

Direct version:

**Control-plane ≠ dashboard.** From source today:

* `control_plane_routing.rs:1-4` — control-plane chat follows its dedicated native agent's configured model. Never dashboard selection, never request override.
* `chat_mode_routing.rs:3-5,19` — ordinary modes use dashboard route, `control_plane` / `accountability` use separate native aliases so they can't inherit the user's picker.

So making Spark the control-plane chatbot doesn't mean flipping the whole picker to Spark. It means:

```
UI -> door :8090 -> resolve mode
  user modes -> dashboard model (Qwen etc, doesn't score)
  control_plane -> dedicated alias -> muse-spark-1.3 (scores)
```

That nails `WINNING.md:20` + `DEMO-STAGING.md:76`: Spark does the reasoning, says so on screen, makes one real tool call through the identity's mount with receipt.

Rendering everything still has one guardrail:

Spark plans + emits **json-render spec only**. Renderer draws only validated spec — `validate_spec` against sealed catalog, reject if fail. No direct HTML/JSX, per your Svelte + json-render stack rule. Menu click = re-render from new spec, not static pages — matches what you wanted.

Steps, design-only:

1. pin `control_plane` native agent route to `muse-spark-1.3`, leave dashboard alone
2. keep Spark call on screen with model field visible, or it doesn't score — Qwen router output doesn't count
3. one Spark tool call via mount `operations/<plugin>/<method>/call` → receipt on screen + refusal demo intact

Want me to draft that control-plane route pin as a proposal — no seal/grant/restart until you approve?

# Subsidiaries and the identity sled

How an identity works as the embodiment of a subsidiary. Marked **existing**
(in 3tched today), **proven** (demonstrated 2026-10-28) or **planned**.

## Hierarchy (owner model)

- **Root**: the 3tched control plane — the only root on the system. Its chatbot is a one-off part of the
  system core, to be fused with the WireGuard server key so it can never be a
  peer (session `<root-session>`). **Planned** — no
  supported re-key operation yet.
- **Root has no execution rights**: it holds authority but executes nothing
  itself; execution is delegated through the execution tracker. A human acting
  as root needs **two approvals** (two-person rule). Today `elevation` offers a
  single-use ticket (`authorize_task`, 60 s TTL); the second approval is new
  work. **Planned.**
- **Owner override** (owner requirement): while the owner is the only human,
  his identity must be able to override the two-approval rule. Proposed:
  routine root actions take two approvals from two independent owner devices
  (session + hardware key/phone); an override is break-glass — fresh
  hardware-key confirmation, a cancellable delay, a receipt anchored on-chain,
  and a notification on a second channel — so even the owner cannot act as
  root silently. A designated human second approver replaces this later.
  **Planned.**
- **Second approver = the control-plane chatbot** (owner decision): it co-signs
  the owner's root actions **by policy, not persuasion** — it receives only a
  structured request (operation, resource, identity, applicable policy), never
  free-text justification; atomic judgments (the chatbot or Jev) feed code that
  decides approve/refuse; anything outside written policy is refused and only
  break-glass can override; every decision is receipted with its reasons. It
  approves but never executes. Tiers: routine = owner + chatbot within policy;
  out of policy = refused, break-glass only; later = human second approver.
  **Planned.**
- **Subsidiaries**: Linux users on the system. Each subsidiary is bounded by
  its home directory. **Planned.**
- **Hackathon subsidiary** (owner, 2026-10-30): a clone of the root chatbot,
  display name `etched::hackathon`, gated on `etched0`. The container exists
  and is stopped. It is not a sled identity yet, and the host mount still
  uses the root session. What to do, and the new / old / changed split:
  [ETCHED-HACKATHON.md](ETCHED-HACKATHON.md). The 2026-10-28 line that the
  subsidiary *is* `3tchedCtlChatbot` described that mount. It is not the
  current owner model.

## What the sled is (existing)

The sled is the identity. For each identity session it holds:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| Record | session id, WireGuard public key, principal kind, genesis hash, trace id, schema version, active flag, timestamps |
| Instance binding | the container that embodies it (name, native UUID, pool) |
| Private leaf | the identity's writable storage, with the canonical subvolumes `@agent_soul`, `@agent_memory`, `@agent_rules`, `@agent_skills`, `@agent_user`, `@agent_shared` (shared/soul read-only; memory/rules/skills/user writable) |
| Session ledger | session events and receipts; the input for vectorization |

Session and principal ids are derived from the public key
(`op-identity::session::derive_session_id` / `derive_principal_id`, Blake3
KDF), so the key, genesis and chain *are* the identity — not a machine.

Lifecycle rules (existing): the identity subsystem owns minting; Cozo owns
assignment; login/start/stop never add or remove Btrfs members; the bridge
only verifies externally mounted storage. Never edit sled rows directly.

## How a subsidiary acts

1. The subsidiary's identity runs in its own container with a 3tchedFS mount
   (lungs). **Proven** for `<subsidiary-session>`.
2. On the host, the same identity's mount is exposed inside the
   subsidiary's home, e.g. `/home/<user>/<Subsidiary>/3tchedfs` and
   `/home/<user>/<Subsidiary>/threetched`, bound to that session
   (`--lungs-session`) with call files owned by that Linux user only
   (call-owner UID). Other users can read schemas but cannot act. **Planned.**
3. Every call: kernel or credential identifies the identity → bridge checks the
   exact capability → MutationEngine commits → receipt. **Proven.**
4. threetched (model/agent) operations used by a subsidiary are its own:
   one router agent per subsidiary with its own model, tool set and budget
   (`max_actions_per_hour`, `max_cost_per_day_cents`). **Planned.**

## Sled + execution tracker (planned)

Every tool call is validated by the one shared execution tracker and written
to the identity's sled session ledger; that ledger is vectorized (Qdrant) so
the identity can answer questions about its own history. Code: branch
`recover/execution-tracker` (`identity_sled_dispatch::subscribe_execution_tracker`).

## Sled + Web3 (planned)

- The index's first entry for an identity records its origin (3tched origin
  session, genesis) and is anchored on-chain.
- A secp256k1 wallet is bound to the identity by a signed link recorded in
  its sled and in the index (the WireGuard key is X25519 and cannot sign
  Ethereum transactions).
- Each index entry references the receipt (`operation_id`, `event_hash`) that
  authorised it.

## Sled + OSCAL boundaries (planned)

The subsidiary's OSCAL profile compiles into: the identity's capability grants
(what it may call), router budgets (how much), and OpenFlow policy on its
network (where it may connect). The bridge already enforces grants on every
call; the new work is generating them from OSCAL.

4. Missing piece I flagged before: FUSE `call -> CallMethod` over WARP-gRPC + catalog/`view.json` projection + state reads + `OutcomeUnknown`/receipt handling + SID1/OIA1 admission for remote peer (not kernel-peer `BindCurrentContainer`). Plus Spark pin needs Meta provider/route in threetched config + service-env key + live `muse-spark-1.3` model-field check — model-list `URLError` still open
5. Then Web3 only if time: origin/genesis anchor + secp256k1 wallet link (WG key can't sign ETH `:90`) + receipt refs `:87-93`

* write the remote-dispatch + Spark control-plane pin as a staged proposal with config authority + verification steps, reusing `etched0` gate + `SUBSIDIARY-SLED` lifecycle, leaving seal/activation/clone-start untouched.

* Remote: 1vCPU/1-2GB, `/dev/fuse` + WireGuard + FUSE frontend only. No Incus leaf, no Btrfs, no sled, no Cozo/Qdrant there.

* Web3 after only if time remains — origin anchor + secp256k1 link, WG key can't sign ETH.

**B. Full subsidiary identity on VPS — not what you asked for**
* Remote: Incus + Btrfs 7-member leaf `@,@agent_*`, sled mint, native UUID, seed pins. `identity_clean_provision.rs:19-27,56-79` is home-specific — pool `/var/lib/incus/storage-pools/3tched-pool`, FSID `a1ab7b42-...`, shared seed, `PLAN_DIR`. 1:# Recovered schema/tag-based routing code
2:
3:Gathered by Codex `/root` on 2026-11-01. Task: `schema-tag-routing-recovery-20261101`.
4:
5:This is a source collection, not a new implementation or a deployment. It contains the recovered schema/tag-routing work, its present source, integration/supporting files, specifications, earlier UI scaffolding, and provenance. Existing shared files contain other contributors' work; their inclusion does not attribute every line to Codex.
6:
7:## Dates and the Btrfs disaster
8:
9:There are two relevant recovery periods. Original Btrfs repair was already underway on **October 9, 2026**. The later preservation/reinstall session was **October 13, 2026**: the VPS was in a forensic live environment, and the conversation explicitly discussed saving uncommitted tag-router work before reinstalling. These establish recovery dates, not a proven exact onset or root cause for every loss.
10:
11:The routing implementation associated with that October 13 recovery was requested on **October 11 at 09:51:36 UTC**, authorized for implementation at **12:49:08 UTC**, and continued **October 12 at 02:19–03:37 UTC**. In America/New_York, the continuation was October 11 at 10:19–11:37 p.m. The original routing thread was `01a129ee-7859-7cd0-8733-2c1ce831d046`; task `schema-tagged-routing-20261011`, OD-06.
12:
13:The eight-hour session description could not be verified from the available originals. A historical recovery assistant estimated two focused periods totaling approximately 3½ hours, while explicitly declining to certify exact active time. The broader routing-mention span was almost 18 hours and included pauses and other work. That estimate does not disprove other long sessions.
14:
15:## What was implemented
16:
17:- `schema_tag_registry.rs` and `_methods.rs`: tag identities/associations, stable-owner policy administration, protected-method markers, canonical mapping references and revision checks.
18:- `routing_decision.rs` and `_methods.rs`: typed private decision records, deterministic gate outcomes, shadow recording and recheck contracts. Tags do not grant capabilities.
19:- `routing_catalog.rs`: resolve exact plugin/method/schema references against a manifest-pinned sealed catalog and recheck after queues.
20:- `routing_dispatch.rs`, `routing_store.rs`, `routing_resources.rs`, `routing-limits.json`: admitted dispatch, private Cozo-backed documents, cancellation/recovery ownership and bounded resource reservations.
21:- `openflow_permit.rs`, `openflow_methods.rs`, controller integration: one-use attributed callbacks and last-moment caller/grant/schema admission for controller writes. This was not complete tag-to-packet enforcement.
22:- `oscal_field_classification.rs` and `_tests.rs`, shared OSCAL registry/dispatch changes: bounded schema-field assessment, inherited reviewed rules, privacy floors and candidate comparison.
23:- `.kiro/specs/schema-tagged-routing/`: requirements, design, phased tasks and explicit unfinished work.
24:
25:The October 11–12 handoffs described a **shadow-only foundation**, not a complete deployed redaction/egress/router lifecycle. Live canonical mapping validation, complete tag-policy enforcement, reviewed field-rule authoring/first-seal publication, full producer preservation, actual redaction and exact-content egress remained outstanding. The historical October 12 GNU check was reported successful; that is not a fresh build/test result. No build, test, seal, deployment, grant or storage change was performed while collecting this file.
26:
27:## Versions and reading order
28:
29:1. **Current source:** backend commit `b77882b915590cbddd68d983535a4ab136c900a8`, captured before this collection. These files include later repairs and renames.
30:2. **Recovered checkpoint:** `7766577e7af741ea227ef1721167cd7dd3cc494f`, committed October 18. This is the earliest retained committed copy found for the new routing modules, not a claim that the work was originally authored October 18. Identical files are cross-referenced; differing historical files are included in full.
31:3. **Earlier UI foundation:** `3tched.com` commit `999651e6d1b9f653d8cf892c390ad1fe22ecfa39`, September 30, with local routing drafts/compliance/accountability scaffolding. Historical React files are archival evidence, not approval to reintroduce that stack into the current application.
32:4. **Changes and history:** a scoped patch from the October 11 committed base to the recovered checkpoint, a patch from the recovered checkpoint to current source, and the selected-path Git history. Checkpoint patches can include other work in shared integration files; they are not exclusively Codex patches or directly applicable to every checkout.
33:
34:Complete files are included for recovery. This subset is not a standalone Cargo workspace; it retains dependencies on the surrounding repository. The late-October `hackathon/catalog-routing` prototype is separate later work and is not attributed to these pre-reinstall Codex sessions.
35:
36:## Evidence and attribution
37:
38:Repository handoffs: `HANDOFF.md` entries dated October 11 12:51, 13:10, 13:32, 13:51 and October 12 02:46/03:44 UTC. They name the new routing modules, OpenFlow integration, field classifier, file ownership and original uncommitted status. The September 30 foundation is documented in `reports/btrfs-cache-memory/20260930-implementation/SESSION-FINAL.md` and `routing/NOTES.md`, included below.
39:
40:Native preservation archive:
41:`/home/jeremy/model-conversations-2026-10-15/codex/sessions/2026/10/13/rollout-2026-10-13T01-19-10-01a133b3-49ba-7a21-b25b-c91424a52ff6.jsonl.zst`.
42:Line numbers refer to decompressed JSONL:
43:
44:- 674: October 13 06:18:26 UTC, forensic live environment/no normal server installed.
45:- 729: October 13 06:20:40 UTC, owner asks how long the tag router was worked on.
46:- 755: recovery tool output quotes original routing record 3115 at October 11 09:51:36 UTC and record 18364 at October 12 03:37:22 UTC.
47:- 770: recovery tool output quotes original record 3938, implementation authorized October 11 12:49:08 UTC.
48:- 762: recovery tool output quotes original record 16987, continuation request October 12 02:19:30 UTC.
49:- 782/818: historical duration estimate and its explicit uncertainty.
50:
51:These are native records of the recovery session, but their quotations of the missing original October 11 root transcript are **secondary evidence**. The prose export also survives at `/home/jeremy/conversation-history-2026-10-15/codex.md`, around lines 101730–101765.
52:
53:The earlier October 9 recovery thread is `01a12009-f007-7fd1-9bc0-dd203ee45f59`; native record 9 at 09:41:39 UTC requests Btrfs repair, and record 81 at 09:43:25 describes device removal/deletion during release preparation. This does not establish a complete forensic cause.
54:
55:The October 13 receipts named `/home/jeremy/Recovery/conversation-audit-20261013/repository/op-dbus-git-and-working-changes.tar` and retained `root-sessions/`. That original backup path is absent on this host today. Therefore the collection uses retained Git objects, not an asserted byte-exact pre-loss working-tree restore. No original transcript, credential or raw private runtime dump is embedded here.
56:
57:The identity mount paths `/run/mounts/3tchedFS` and `/run/mount/3tchedFS` were absent during collection. NotebookLM retrieval/sync was unavailable through that surface; no alternate identity or backend transport was used. Source and authorized local historical records provided the evidence.

# Recovered schema/tag-based routing code

Gathered by Codex `/root` on 2026-11-01. Task: `schema-tag-routing-recovery-20261101`.

This is a source collection, not a new implementation or a deployment. It contains the recovered schema/tag-routing work, its present source, integration/supporting files, specifications, earlier UI scaffolding, and provenance. Existing shared files contain other contributors' work; their inclusion does not attribute every line to Codex.

## Dates and the Btrfs disaster

There are two relevant recovery periods. Original Btrfs repair was already underway on **October 9, 2026**. The later preservation/reinstall session was **October 13, 2026**: the VPS was in a forensic live environment, and the conversation explicitly discussed saving uncommitted tag-router work before reinstalling. These establish recovery dates, not a proven exact onset or root cause for every loss.

The routing implementation associated with that October 13 recovery was requested on **October 11 at 09:51:36 UTC**, authorized for implementation at **12:49:08 UTC**, and continued **October 12 at 02:19–03:37 UTC**. In America/New_York, the continuation was October 11 at 10:19–11:37 p.m. The original routing thread was `01a129ee-7859-7cd0-8733-2c1ce831d046`; task `schema-tagged-routing-20261011`, OD-06.

The eight-hour session description could not be verified from the available originals. A historical recovery assistant estimated two focused periods totaling approximately 3½ hours, while explicitly declining to certify exact active time. The broader routing-mention span was almost 18 hours and included pauses and other work. That estimate does not disprove other long sessions.

## What was implemented

- `schema_tag_registry.rs` and `_methods.rs`: tag identities/associations, stable-owner policy administration, protected-method markers, canonical mapping references and revision checks.
- `routing_decision.rs` and `_methods.rs`: typed private decision records, deterministic gate outcomes, shadow recording and recheck contracts. Tags do not grant capabilities.
- `routing_catalog.rs`: resolve exact plugin/method/schema references against a manifest-pinned sealed catalog and recheck after queues.
- `routing_dispatch.rs`, `routing_store.rs`, `routing_resources.rs`, `routing-limits.json`: admitted dispatch, private Cozo-backed documents, cancellation/recovery ownership and bounded resource reservations.
- `openflow_permit.rs`, `openflow_methods.rs`, controller integration: one-use attributed callbacks and last-moment caller/grant/schema admission for controller writes. This was not complete tag-to-packet enforcement.
- `oscal_field_classification.rs` and `_tests.rs`, shared OSCAL registry/dispatch changes: bounded schema-field assessment, inherited reviewed rules, privacy floors and candidate comparison.
- `.kiro/specs/schema-tagged-routing/`: requirements, design, phased tasks and explicit unfinished work.

The October 11–12 handoffs described a **shadow-only foundation**, not a complete deployed redaction/egress/router lifecycle. Live canonical mapping validation, complete tag-policy enforcement, reviewed field-rule authoring/first-seal publication, full producer preservation, actual redaction and exact-content egress remained outstanding. The historical October 12 GNU check was reported successful; that is not a fresh build/test result. No build, test, seal, deployment, grant or storage change was performed while collecting this file.

## Versions and reading order

1. **Current source:** backend commit `b77882b915590cbddd68d983535a4ab136c900a8`, captured before this collection. These files include later repairs and renames.
2. **Recovered checkpoint:** `7766577e7af741ea227ef1721167cd7dd3cc494f`, committed October 18. This is the earliest retained committed copy found for the new routing modules, not a claim that the work was originally authored October 18. Identical files are cross-referenced; differing historical files are included in full.
3. **Earlier UI foundation:** `3tched.com` commit `999651e6d1b9f653d8cf892c390ad1fe22ecfa39`, September 30, with local routing drafts/compliance/accountability scaffolding. Historical React files are archival evidence, not approval to reintroduce that stack into the current application.
4. **Changes and history:** a scoped patch from the October 11 committed base to the recovered checkpoint, a patch from the recovered checkpoint to current source, and the selected-path Git history. Checkpoint patches can include other work in shared integration files; they are not exclusively Codex patches or directly applicable to every checkout.

Complete files are included for recovery. This subset is not a standalone Cargo workspace; it retains dependencies on the surrounding repository. The late-October `hackathon/catalog-routing` prototype is separate later work and is not attributed to these pre-reinstall Codex sessions.

## Evidence and attribution

Repository handoffs: `HANDOFF.md` entries dated October 11 12:51, 13:10, 13:32, 13:51 and October 12 02:46/03:44 UTC. They name the new routing modules, OpenFlow integration, field classifier, file ownership and original uncommitted status. The September 30 foundation is documented in `reports/btrfs-cache-memory/20260930-implementation/SESSION-FINAL.md` and `routing/NOTES.md`, included below.

Native preservation archive:
`/home/jeremy/model-conversations-2026-10-15/codex/sessions/2026/10/13/rollout-2026-10-13T01-19-10-01a133b3-49ba-7a21-b25b-c91424a52ff6.jsonl.zst`.
Line numbers refer to decompressed JSONL:

- 674: October 13 06:18:26 UTC, forensic live environment/no normal server installed.
- 729: October 13 06:20:40 UTC, owner asks how long the tag router was worked on.
- 755: recovery tool output quotes original routing record 3115 at October 11 09:51:36 UTC and record 18364 at October 12 03:37:22 UTC.
- 770: recovery tool output quotes original record 3938, implementation authorized October 11 12:49:08 UTC.
- 762: recovery tool output quotes original record 16987, continuation request October 12 02:19:30 UTC.
- 782/818: historical duration estimate and its explicit uncertainty.

These are native records of the recovery session, but their quotations of the missing original October 11 root transcript are **secondary evidence**. The prose export also survives at `/home/jeremy/conversation-history-2026-10-15/codex.md`, around lines 101730–101765.

The earlier October 9 recovery thread is `01a12009-f007-7fd1-9bc0-dd203ee45f59`; native record 9 at 09:41:39 UTC requests Btrfs repair, and record 81 at 09:43:25 describes device removal/deletion during release preparation. This does not establish a complete forensic cause.

The October 13 receipts named `/home/jeremy/Recovery/conversation-audit-20261013/repository/op-dbus-git-and-working-changes.tar` and retained `root-sessions/`. That original backup path is absent on this host today. Therefore the collection uses retained Git objects, not an asserted byte-exact pre-loss working-tree restore. No original transcript, credential or raw private runtime dump is embedded here.

The identity mount paths `/run/mounts/3tchedFS` and `/run/mount/3tchedFS` were absent during collection. NotebookLM retrieval/sync was unavailable through that surface; no alternate identity or backend transport was used. Source and authorized local historical records provided the evidence.

# catalog-routing

Pure request routing over nested catalogs: `routing/DATA-MODEL.md` as code.
No I/O, no network.

- `catalogs/compliance` — control tags → OSCAL controls → candidate plugin
  operations (`oscal/TAG-TAXONOMY.md`; `oscal/` JSON is authoritative).
- `catalogs/ui` — component support per renderer target
  (`docs/DROP-IN-SPEC.md` §2.1; the sealed `json_render` blob is authoritative).
- `catalogs/models` — provider/model selection over a caller-supplied registry
  (the live `chat_router` catalog is authoritative; this crate only matches).
- `decide` — allow / refuse (naming the missing capability) / needs-approval
  (root: two humans, mirroring the `approvals/` crate).

1://! The EMQX doorbell: sled-gated, content-free wakes for private views.
2://!
3://! Owner decisions (2026-09-19): no broker ACL tables, no MCP over MQTT, no
4://! authoritative state on the broker; SHM is the one truth. So the broker
5://! carries exactly one thing per commit — `{"seq": <revision>}` on
6://! `opdbus/wake/<owner-key>` — and every verdict here is a *function of the
7://! identity the client presented*, never a lookup in a policy table:
8://!
9://! * A doorbell client's MQTT client id **is** its owner key
10://!   (`sha256(principal, session, genesis)`, the same key the private
11://!   episode view uses). The broker never sees a principal, session, or key.
12://! * `client.authenticate`: the password is one of the door's two
13://!   credentials — the inline SID1 (`sid1:…`, provisioned container/agent
14://!   sessions) or the OIA1 assertion the decoy issued (`oia1:<base64>`, the
15://!   browser). Each is verified exactly as the door verifies it (sled match
16://!   with the `mqtt` transport scope, or signature/lifetime/replay/source
17://!   binding plus the anchored human session), must belong to an unrevoked
18://!   registered principal, and must derive exactly the client id.
19://! * `client.authorize`: a doorbell client may only SUBSCRIBE to its own
20://!   topic, and only while some anchored, unexpired sled still derives its
21://!   client id (re-checked on every subscribe). Every other client is denied
22://!   the `opdbus/` namespace and otherwise left to the broker's own rules.
23://!
24://! Revocation: tombstoning a sled makes the next subscribe fail, and the
25://! bridge kicks the owner key's connection through `emqx.kick_client`.

Assessment: neither replaces canonical mapping — they flank it.

**Plan I ran:** locate EMQX wake path + OpenFlow enforcement + pure decide, rank, read headers — no changes.

| Option | What it actually does in source | Fit for tag-routing |
|---|---|---|
| EMQX | ExHook audit tap, `IGNORE` — publish decisions left to broker, gating stays on plugin surface (`emqx_hook_provider.rs:5-12`). Only exception is doorbell: sled-gated, content-free `{"seq":revision}` on `opdbus/wake/<owner-key>`, client id = owner key, SID1/OIA1 auth, own topic only (`wake_doorbell.rs:1-22`). SHM is one truth, broker carries no state | wakes/notify only — e.g. chat turn wakes, decision-ready notify. Can't allow/deny `plugin/method` calls, can't see PII/tags |
| OpenFlow | L2-L4 flows via `op-of-controller`, `FlowEntry/FlowAction` schema, `observed_flows` is observation never replaces authored config (`openflow.rs:51-56`). `openflow_permit` = one-use attributed callbacks + last-moment grant/schema admission — tag-to-packet was never complete (`SCHEMA:21`) | where-packets-go, not what-operation-means. Good for `etched0` isolation / `hackbr0` egress, can't match OSCAL tags, field PII, method args |
| Combo | canonical decides → EMQX wakes private view → OpenFlow contains network | valid defense-in-depth, still needs canonical as base you locked |

For Wed: keep routing = canonical OSCAL→sealed-object mapping + pure `catalog-routing/decide` (allow / refuse-with-cap / needs-approval). Use EMQX only for its proven chat wakes, OpenFlow only for the existing `etched0` gate. Tag-driven flows or MQTT-enforced calls are new scope — would miss the deadline and break freeze.

Extracted 2026-11-01 from `SCHEMA-TAG-ROUTING-CODE.md` (Codex collection,
`schema-tag-routing-recovery-20261101`) and re-verified against the **live tree
at HEAD `b77882b915590cbddd68d983535a4ab136c900a8`** — after the bridge rewrite
(`server.rs` / `grpc_server.rs` / `lib.rs`) and after chat messaging moved to
EMQX (doorbell + ExHook only, see Tier 4).

**Ranking key:** Tier 1 = byte-identical to live, sealed, callable today.
Descending tiers = still-present but partial/proposed, then context-only, then
stale/archival — do not build on the bottom tiers without re-verification.

**Verification:** Jev `judge_batch jdgb-15bcd9276f1a435b` (jev-1.14.0).
Jev scores `< 0.6` are *inconclusive* per repo rule and are labelled as such;
those verdicts rest on the primary evidence cited (exact SHA-256 matches and
grep call-paths), with Jev only corroborative. No build/test/seal was run.

---

## Tier 1 — Strongest: live, sealed, byte-identical routing core

Evidence: live `sha256sum` matches the collection's `current-20261101` index
exactly, and both plugins are sealed in the live catalog
(72 blobs, incl. `routing_decision.e8c810cd666d3189.blob`,
`schema_tag_registry.efda4ac1ab2e6a22.blob`).

| `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/routing_decision.rs` | `b789f779d7430322b47b7eb3f585c8e15f131742a9a6df9e6fa61c72f0a6b9cf` |

### 1.1 How you call it (the only usage path)

No public Rust API, no chat/EMQX entry point. A caller uses the sealed plugin
methods through `PluginService.CallMethod` (door `:8090`) or 3tchedFS
`operations/<plugin>/<method>/call`, with the exact capability held.
`MutationEngine` reserves routing capacity *before* parsing untrusted args,
then dispatches:

```rust
// crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/mutation_engine.rs:3592-3594
let early_routing = crate::routing_dispatch::reserve_before_parse(
    self, plugin_id, method, capability_id, actor_id, session_id, session_genesis,
).await?;

// crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/mutation_engine.rs:3800-3813
"routing_decision" | "schema_tag_registry" => {
    crate::routing_dispatch::dispatch(
        self, plugin_id, method, &serde_json::to_value(&parsed_value)?,
        actor_id, capability_id, session_id, session_genesis,
        &admitted_schema, &change.change_id,
        routing_admission.context("routing owner reservation missing")?,
    ).await?
}
```

```rust
// crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/routing_dispatch.rs:1-4,88,239
//! Admitted dispatch for private schema-tag and shadow-decision documents.
//! This first slice records proposals only. It never installs forwarding,
//! claims an execution receipt, or treats a recorded allow as a credential.
pub(crate) async fn dispatch(
    engine: &MutationEngine, plugin: &str, method: &str,
    args: &serde_json::Value, actor: &str, capability: Option<&str>,
    session: Option<&str>, genesis: Option<&str>,
    admitted: &PluginSchema, operation_id: &str,
    reservation: RoutingAdmission,
) -> Result<serde_json::Value>
pub(crate) async fn reserve_before_parse(/* … */)
    -> Result<Option<(PluginSchema, RoutingAdmission)>>
```

Final admission inside dispatch re-checks the caller and the catalog after
any queueing (`routing_dispatch.rs:37-81`): `chat_router_admission::readmit_call`
(an admission helper — *not* chat transport), then
`routing_catalog::recheck(operation)` and association re-resolution.

### 1.2 Methods you can call today

From `routing_decision_schema()` (`routing_decision.rs:99-119`) and
`schema_tag_registry_schema()` (`schema_tag_registry.rs:114-183`):

| Plugin.method | Effect | Required capability | Subid |

| `routing_decision.get_decision` | Read | `cap.governance.routing-decision.read@v1` | `obs.software.routing-decision.get@v1` |
| `routing_decision.record_shadow_decision` | Mutation | `cap.governance.routing-decision.record@v1` | `mut.software.routing-decision.record-shadow@v1` |
| `schema_tag_registry.list_tags` / `get_tag` / `get_protected_method_marker` / `list_policies` / `get_policy` | Read | `cap.governance.schema-tag-registry.read@v1` | `obs.software.schema-tag-registry.*@v1` |
| `schema_tag_registry.register_tag_semantics` | Mutation | `cap.governance.schema-tag-registry.tag.register@v1` | `mut.software.schema-tag-registry.register-tag-semantics@v1` |
| `schema_tag_registry.set_protected_method_marker` | Mutation | `cap.governance.schema-tag-registry.marker.set@v1` | `mut.software.schema-tag-registry.set-protected-marker@v1` |
| `schema_tag_registry.author_policy` / `update_policy` / `revoke_policy` | Mutation | `cap.governance.schema-tag-registry.policy.{author,update,revoke}@v1` | `mut.software.schema-tag-registry.*-policy@v1` |

### 1.3 Catalog resolution (complete, self-contained)

// crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/routing_catalog.rs:14-48 (abridged; full file is 81 lines)

    let operation = ResolvedOperationRef { /* plugin_id, method_key, transport_name,
        schema_hash, schema_version, catalog_hash, subid, required_capability */ };
    operation.validate()?;
    Ok(operation)
}

# catalog-routing

Pure request routing over nested catalogs: `routing/DATA-MODEL.md` as code.
No I/O, no network.

- `catalogs/compliance` — control tags → OSCAL controls → candidate plugin
  operations (`oscal/TAG-TAXONOMY.md`; `oscal/` JSON is authoritative).
- `catalogs/ui` — component support per renderer target
  (`docs/DROP-IN-SPEC.md` §2.1; the sealed `json_render` blob is authoritative).
- `catalogs/models` — provider/model selection over a caller-supplied registry
  (the live `chat_router` catalog is authoritative; this crate only matches).
- `decide` — allow / refuse (naming the missing capability) / needs-approval
  (root: two humans, mirroring the `approvals/` crate).

## Plan (10 days)
…

## Known open issues

- ~~Meta model not wired~~ — resolved 2026-10-28: Meta's Model API (`https://api.meta.ai/v1`, `muse-spark-1.3`) is wired for development (`~/.bash_secrets`) and the running service (`/home/3tched/.config/etched/env`); see `docs/RUNTIME.md`. 3tched's own chat router still uses a Qwen model.
- Router turn costs ~15k tokens (skills bundle removed to halve it). Qwen does
  not reliably emit text tool calls. (MCP is retired — replaced by the 3tchedFS
  mount — so do not rely on the router's MCP tools.)
- Live state reads through the mount (`plugins/*/value.json`) return EIO.
- Next release will fail activation: `notebook-sources-sync` cannot pass its
  30 s check after restart. Fix before releasing.
- Re-key of the core chatbot to the WireGuard server key (session
  `<root-session>`) has no supported op yet.
- UI overlay on `dashboard-release` is runtime-only; lost on reboot or release.

## CMS: compliant by construction (owner direction, 2026-10-28)

The CMS is the showcase because it comes out usable *and* evidently
controlled. Pick a handful of controls whose effect is visible on stage; each
control → a CMS behaviour → evidence (receipt or anchor):

| Control area | Visible behaviour | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| PII handling (NIST 800-53 PT) | automatic redaction on publish; original kept only in the owner's private scope | redaction operation receipt naming the triggering policy |
| Audit (AU) | every create/edit/publish attributable | receipt chain: who, capability, when |
| Access control (AC) | roles compiled into capability grants | a live denial showing the exact missing capability |
| Retention (SI-12) | scheduled expiry/archive | scheduled operation receipt |
| Integrity | published versions hash-anchored | on-chain anchor a judge can check |

Pitch wording: "implements and evidences these controls" — never "compliant"
or "certified" (an assessor declares compliance).

## Remote identities: established design (owner, 2026-10-28)

WireGuard is only the establishment step: the peer key proves the identity
once, the decoy issues the signed peer proof (OIA1) and the session gets its
sealed credential (SID1). After that it is zero trust — every call carries the
credential and the door's interceptor re-verifies it, over any transport
(internet, Cloudflare). 3tched-fs `Credential` mode is the remote form of the
lungs. The mechanism exists; it needs testing and refinement, not a rebuild.
Do not add a mesh (Netmaker/Cloudflare) as an identity layer.

## Progress log

- 2026-10-28: Junie pinned to Muse Spark for this repo — new
  `.junie/config.json` sets `model: muse-spark-1.3`, `effort: medium`

arguments.content:
# cms

Drop-in CMS: usable *and* evidently controlled. Pitch wording: "implements
and evidences these controls" — never "compliant" or "certified".

Each control → CMS behaviour → evidence. Status is honest: **crate-proven**
means covered by `catalog-routing` unit tests in this repo; **stage-gated**
means proven only by a live mount read + receipt on rehearsal day.

| Control area | Visible behaviour | Evidence | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| PII handling (PT) | automatic redaction on publish; original stays in owner's private scope | redaction receipt naming the triggering policy | crate-proven detector + masker (`redaction`); live receipt stage-gated |
| Audit (AU) | every create/edit/publish attributable | receipt chain: who, capability, when | crate-proven decision records; live chain stage-gated |
| Access control (AC) | roles compiled into capability grants | live denial naming the exact missing capability | crate-proven (`decide` refuse paths + route pins); live denial stage-gated |
| Retention (SI-12) | scheduled expiry/archive | scheduled operation receipt | planned — off the Wed run unless proven |
| Integrity | published versions hash-anchored | on-chain anchor a judge can check | planned — off the Wed run unless proven |

Routing in: end-user `WorkflowPurpose` (promoted tags, closed taxonomy
values) → `decide` allow / refuse / needs-approval → Spark `muse-spark-1.3`
spec → `validate_spec` vs sealed catalog → renderer draws only validated
refs. Publish path adds the deterministic screen first, JEV semantic
screen second, fail-closed both; publish stays off the run unless its
masking receipt proves out.
